- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.

Sample text:
---
The summer my mother retired, she began returning things. Not purchases, which she had always returned with the receipt folded neatly around the offending button or cracked lid, but objects that had lived in our house for decades. A blue casserole went to Mrs. Vale across town. A pair of binoculars went to a man who had moved to Oregon. From the linen closet came a yellow towel with MARTIN written on its hem. Nobody remembered Martin. My mother washed the towel, pressed it, and laid it on the dining room table as if expecting him to arrive before lunch.

I was staying with her while my apartment building acquired new plumbing and, according to increasingly optimistic notices, a water supply. Every morning over coffee I received an assignment. Find out whether the Vale daughter still taught piano. See what postage to Oregon would cost. Look through the school photographs for a boy called Martin, possibly a swimmer. I asked what had brought this on. She tipped the sugar bowl toward herself, although she took her coffee black, and studied the small white slope inside. “I have spent thirty years,” she said, “looking around this place for a decent screwdriver.”

This seemed less an explanation than a fresh assignment. Nevertheless, the work agreed with me. Calling strangers with good news is a pleasure ordinarily reserved for people who award grants. The binoculars, it turned out, had belonged to a birdwatcher who was now nearly blind. His granddaughter wrote to say that he wanted them anyway. Mrs. Vale received her casserole without emotion but sent back six peaches in a paper sack, each peach wrapped separately in a page from the sporting section. We ate them standing at the sink. Juice ran down our wrists. The home team had lost again.

By August the dining room held only the towel. We had identified three Martins, none of whom wanted it. One explained at considerable length that his family had always used green towels because his mother believed yellow attracted wasps. Another offered to take it if we were in a bind. The third had been dead since February; his husband answered my letter in a careful hand, enclosing a photograph of Martin at the beach. He was a slight man wearing enormous sunglasses, and over his shoulder, blurred but unmistakable, hung a white hotel towel with a narrow stripe of blue.

“Maybe Martin was the brand,” I suggested. My mother looked insulted. She knew the difference between a manufacturer's label and a name written by a parent, she said. Manufacturers did not go back over the M when the ink ran thin. I picked up the hem. She was right. That awkward first mountain had been climbed twice. I thought of somebody bending over a kitchen counter before camp, already late for work, holding the cloth taut with one hand. Perhaps a child had stood beside that person eating cereal. Perhaps he had said, Nobody's going to steal my stupid towel.

That afternoon the plumber called. There was water in my kitchen again, though for the moment hot came from both taps. I packed my books and carried them downstairs. In the garage my mother was sitting on an overturned bucket, dismantling a wooden box that had once held Christmas ornaments. Beside her lay a screwdriver with a handsome amber handle. “Where did that come from?” I asked. “Hardware store,” she said. “Four dollars.” She passed me the lid of the box. On the underside, in her own handwriting, was a list of gifts from the year I had turned nine.

Among the usual entries, socks and puzzles and a book about whales, was one item I could not account for: a front door key. At nine I had been too young to come home alone. My mother reminded me that I used to go outside after supper and ring the bell, sometimes a dozen times in an evening. I liked the sound, but more than that I liked the ceremony of being admitted. Eventually she had given me a key so she could finish a meal. Had it worked? She laughed. “You unlocked the door and rang the bell anyway.”

I took the lid upstairs. In the empty dining room the late light had found a flaw in the windowpane and projected a little crooked rainbow onto the wall. I folded the yellow towel around the lid to keep its splintered edge from catching on my clothes. My mother came in as I was leaving. For a moment I expected an objection. Instead she tucked a loose corner under my arm. “Give me a call when you get there,” she said, although my apartment was twelve minutes away and she could practically see the roof of it from her porch.

The apartment smelled of plaster. I opened the windows, set the box lid on a shelf, and carried the towel to the bathroom. There was a small puddle under the sink. I got down on my knees and dried the floor, working the towel around the pipe and into the narrow dusty space behind the pedestal. When I stood up, a streak of rust crossed the yellow cotton. I felt unexpectedly ashamed, as though I had put a wedding dress to work polishing silver. Then another drop gathered on the pipe. I spread the towel underneath and called my mother.

She answered on the first ring. In the background I could hear the radio playing the shipping forecast, a program she enjoyed despite living nowhere near navigable water. I told her about the leak and the rust. “Well,” she said, “it was never much good for drying yourself. Too thin.” Outside, somebody was trying to parallel park a truck, and a stranger on the pavement had stopped to guide him. A little more, the stranger said, come on, you've got room. I sat on the bathroom floor and watched the yellow darken, listening to my mother's weather for distant boats.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld
Source model: `withheld`
Condition: MID

## Sample kind
GENRE_FICTION — A literary domestic short story built around a recurring object and a gradual emotional revelation.

## Grounded reading
The voice is wry, observant, and quietly tender, finding feeling in practical details rather than declarations. The towel, the key, and the mother’s assignments turn ordinary acts of sorting and returning into a story about belonging, usefulness, and being welcomed home. Its pathos comes through small gestures—the towel tucked under the narrator’s arm, the call answered on the first ring—and invites the reader to notice how care can persist in habits and objects.

## What the model chose to foreground
The story foregrounds an aging household, objects that carry traces of absent people, and the difference between an object’s usefulness and its emotional value. It makes the mother’s returns a route toward the narrator’s childhood ritual of ringing the bell to be admitted, then brings that pattern into the present through the leaking sink and the call home. The mood stays gently comic and bittersweet, with care expressed as practical attention.

## Evidence line
> I felt unexpectedly ashamed, as though I had put a wedding dress to work polishing silver.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The recurring objects and restrained emotional turns give this sample a coherent, distinctive sensibility, especially in how it makes ordinary usefulness carry affection.
